title: What is Zen, Part 3
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona and Nyogen Connie Martin
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona and Nyogen Connie Martin take up Sangha, the third of the three treasures, through Norman Fischer and Susan Moon's book What is Zen. Heigaku reads Norman on practicing together, and Nyogen tells of the young monk Meghiya, who asks three times to meditate in a cool mango grove and is overrun there by unskillful thoughts. The Buddha's answer begins with admirable friends. Nyogen then reads Ananda calling friendship half of the holy life and the Buddha correcting that it is the whole, and listeners pair up for active listening on Susan's question about someone who likes sangha potlucks more than zazen.

In some stretches the recording does not show which of them is speaking, so those passages carry no new label.]*
**Heigaku Talus Latona:** Hello.
If anyone needs to move closer, please feel free to pull your chairs up.
The three treasures are mentioned in the very earliest Buddhist teachings that we find: Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Continuing with the theme of this month, we're following Norman Fischer and Susan Moon's book on what is Zen.

Tonight we are delving into Sangha, which we translate as community and which, in very traditional terms, refers only to the community of monks practicing Zen in the monastery and the Theravada tradition.
It expands in the Mahayana tradition to include all living beings and nonliving beings, all sentient beings.
As Norman points out, Dogen includes roof tiles and rivers.
On the question of what is Sangha, Norman points us to examine from relative and absolute perspectives.
*He says, to really be able in a healthy way to be a member of a concrete Sangha, you need to see that the people in the room are not limited to the people in the room.
In these few are the many, and to really love one person or one group of people is, in truth, to love everyone.
This is an impossible ideal, but it is something we always have to keep in mind and heart and aspire to.*
Jisan Tova Green at San Francisco's City Zen Center writes:
*When I first encountered Zen students at a Buddhist Peace Fellowship gathering, I was impressed by their warmth, openness and uprightness.
I wanted to be like them.
I began sitting with them at Berkeley Zen Center and Green Gulch Farm.
This was before I knew about Kuan Yin, but she was manifesting through the lives of my Zen friends.
I first heard about fish basket Kuan Yin on a pilgrimage to Kuan Yin sacred sites in China, led by Aijun Linda Cutts and Rusa Chui in 2005.*
Jisan continues:

*My teacher Aijun Linda Cutts encourages students to copy, memorize and recite texts we study with her, and memorizing the parable of the herbs in the Lotus Sutra, I was drawn to its message of rain falling equally on all plants and trees, large and small alike, giving each what it needs.
The Buddhist teachings are available to everyone, no matter their age, race, class, gender or sexual orientation.
This parable helps me appreciate the uniqueness of each member in our sangha, including those who are very different from me.

It also helps me to be friendly when I open the front door, not knowing whether I will be greeting the UPS delivery person, or a homeless man or woman, asking for food, or a sangha member coming for a class.*
So why do we practice in sangha, rather than sitting in front of the door?
Rather than, say, as a hermit?
Why did monks group into monasteries?
There certainly are alone hermit practices.

For me, personally, besides the shared aspiration and practices with true communication that Jisan Tova Green refers to, the variety and how everyone in this awe-inspiring group sees the world pollinates my thinking.
Koans, for example, aren't just a question with the right answer.
Many insights and ideas brought up by fellow students have kindled deep chains of understanding for me.
And looking at the why of Sangha, Norman writes:
*Practicing together in harmonious community without emphasizing individuality expands your sense of self to include others.
It makes you appreciate your individuality not as something unique and better than or worse than that of others, but rather as an expression of something fundamental and universal in human beings.
It's one thing to have this idea and another to literally train in it every day in the Zendo.
In Zen practice, the effort is to let go of the self concept and live from the gut, from the breath, from the body, that is from our inmost non-conceptual, unforced individuality.
Just ourselves as we are without posturing, what a relief.*
Connie, tell us a story.
**Nyogen Connie Martin:** One of the early suttas from the Buddha has to do with a young monk named Magia.
It's called the Magia Sutta, actually, and I love this story.
This young monk is so enthusiastic and so [unclear: "long-headed"] and so open to learning that he is just, I think, wonderful.
In the beginning of the sutta it says:
*I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Kalinkas at Kalinka Mountain.
On that occasion, Venerable Magia was the Buddha's attendant.
Then Venerable Magia went to the Blessed One and on arrival, having bowed down to him, stood to one side.
As he was standing there, he said, I would like to go into Jantung Village for alms.*
So he wants to go into town begging for food.
The Buddha gives him permission and Magia goes into the village, begs for food, comes back, eats his meal, but on the way back he notices a mango grove.
Imagine this is India where it's [unclear: "blue-stirring"] hot outside and there's this cool, dark shade under a mango grove.
I actually saw this one time in Mexico.
I went to Mardajada for a retreat that Norman was leading.
I took a hike up into the hills above the resort and there was a mango grove up there.
I remember how hot it was now, how cool and dark that shade looked.
Unfortunately, it was fenced off so I couldn't go sit under a mango tree, but I remember that it looked really wonderful.
So for Magia, he's walking up and down along the bank of the river to exercise and he saw this mango grove and the thought occurred to him:
*How pleasing and charming this mango grove is.
It's enough for a young man of good family intent on [unclear: "exact"] himself in meditation.
If the Blessed One will give me permission, I will come back here and sit meditation in this mango grove.*
So he goes to the Blessed One, to the Buddha, and asks permission to go and sit in the mango grove.
The Buddha only has this one attendant at that point and he says, "Magia, I think you should stay here with me."
But then Magia points out, you know, you're enlightened, you've done it already.
I still have a lot of work to do, so could I please go sit in this mango grove and meditate?
The Buddha puts him off again, and then after the third time he asks, the Buddha says, okay, Magia, go do what you think you have to do.
And Magia goes to the mango grove and finds a beautiful tree to sit under.
Where am I?
Let's see.
So Magia sits down, and to his surprise, he was assaulted by all kinds of unskillful thoughts.
Thoughts of sensuality, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of doing harm.
The thought occurred to him.
And again, this is his youthful [unclear: "mango"], this is his great enthusiasm, and he says:
*How amazing, how astounding.
Even though it was through faith that I went forth from home to the homeless state and the homeless life, still I am overpowered by these three kinds of unskillful thoughts.
Thoughts of sensuality, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of doing harm.*
So he comes back from the mango grove and goes to the Buddha and again says, how amazing, how astounding.
Even though it was through faith that I went forth, blah, blah, blah.
And the Buddha responds finally:
*Magia, in one whose awareness release is still immature, five qualities bring it to maturity.
Which five?
There's a case where a monk has admirable people as friends, companions, and colleagues.
In one whose awareness release is still immature, this is the first quality that brings it to maturity.*
So the first quality that is needed is having admirable people as friends, companions, and colleagues.
And the Buddha goes through some other qualities that are necessary.
The monk must be virtuous.
*[Heigaku Talus Latona and Nyogen Connie Martin share this talk.

In some stretches the recording does not show which of them is speaking, so those passages carry no new label.]*
*He gets to hear at will, easily and without difficulty, talk that is truly sobering and conducive to the opening of awareness.
He keeps his persistence aroused for abandoning unskillful thoughts.
Furthermore, he is discerning, endowed with a discernment related to arising and passing away.
Magia, in one whose awareness release is still immature, these are the five qualities that bring it to maturity.*
But then the Buddha repeats those same qualities again.
In front of each quality that he recites, he begins with the first one.
*There's a case where a monk has admirable people as friends, companions, and colleagues.
In one whose awareness release is still immature, this is the first quality that brings it to maturity.*
So that's basically the whole of the Magia Sutta.
Let's see if I have anything else here I wanted to say.
I have a note here that says Norman sees spiritual friendship as central to the path, and sees spiritual friendship as taking place in the context of community.
So we don't find that just sitting on our cushions at home.
It has to come up and be shared in a group like the one here now.
So that's Magia.
Isn't he wonderful?
I just think he's great.
Okay, over to you.
**Heigaku Talus Latona:** So, down from the value of practicing the sangha to the value of friendship.
Though Norman is a famous Zen teacher, in the book What is Zen, Reigetsu Susan Moon offers tremendous teachings through her setting up the questions that Norman answers.
She takes up the question of belonging and friendship in the sangha, asking:
*I've heard people say they went to practice zazen at a Zen center for months without anyone ever greeting them.
Some people like this because they don't have to chit chat.
And after zazen, they can just leave and get on with their day.
But some people feel lonely and left out when this happens.*
Norman says:
*When you come to a Zen place, you will sense the quiet and the invitation to practice silence as much as and probably more than the offer for friendship.
Which is there too, of course.
The friendship and support generally come later, naturally, as you warm up to the place.
In my years of Zen practice, I have encountered many practitioners who have come for and have been healed by community.
Spiritual communities, like other communities, are basically just people doing something together.
But in spiritual community, there is an explicit commitment to sharing life with whoever comes to do the practice.
This is essential to the Buddhist idea of sangha.
Whoever comes is a member of the community.
Zen isn't really about zazen and koans.
It is about how we live, who we are, and how we treat others.*
Well, appreciating the grin on Connie's face when she talks about Magia.
Talk about somebody else, if you would.
**Nyogen Connie Martin:** Ananda.
The Buddha's longtime companion.
Ananda listened to all of the Buddha's words and memorized everything.
And there is a sutta in which Ananda talks to the Buddha about friendship.
It's actually very short and very clear.
Ananda asks the Buddha, wondering whether having good friends is even as much as half of the path, the Buddhist path.
The Buddha makes it very clear that he values sangha and actually considers sangha practice to be the whole of the Buddhist path.
*I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was living among the Sakians.
Now there is a Sakian town named Sakara.
There, Venerable Ananda went to the Blessed One and on arrival, having bowed down to the Blessed One, sat to one side.
As he was sitting there, Ananda said to the Blessed One, "This is half of the holy life, Lord: admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie."*
*"Don't say that, Ananda.
Don't say that.
Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.
When a monk is admirable to people, his friends, companions, and comrades, it can be expected, she can be expected, to develop and pursue the noble eightfold path.*
*And how does a monk who has admirable people, his friends, companions, and comrades, develop and pursue the noble eightfold path?
There is a case where a monk develops right view dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on [unclear: "secession"], resulting in relinquishment.

He develops right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on [unclear: "secession"], resulting in relinquishment.
This is how a monk who has admirable people, his friends, companions, and colleagues, develops and pursues the noble eightfold path."*
So the monk, or the person, whoever it is, is able to pursue the noble eightfold path.
And all these things like right speech, right resolve, right action, right livelihood, because he has companions and colleagues to help him or her.
*And through this line of reasoning, one may know how admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie,* these things are always very repetitive, *the whole of the holy life.

It is [unclear: "independence on me"] as an admirable friend that brings subject to birth and having gained release from birth, that brings subject to aging, have gained release from aging, that brings subject to death, having gained release from death, that brings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, have gained release from sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair.
It's through this line of reasoning that one may know how admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie, is actually the whole of the holy life.*
So that's the Buddha responding to Ananda, who was thinking that sangha is half of the holy life.
The Buddha is saying, no, it's the whole of the holy life.
It's all of it.
Please count off from one through seven.
Two.
Three.
Four.
Five.
Six.
Seven.
Okay, so if those people would identify who it is that has the same number as them, continuing on with one.
One.
Two.
Six.
Seven.
Now, go join up with the person that has the same number as you.
Number three.
Oh, I am.
Oh, how did that happen?
Well, it just happened.
I'm with one of your numbers.
Why don't you two go together then?
I'm going to count off.
You two go together.
Okay.
Yeah, I'm joining you two.
I am the [unclear: "virgin"] between you two.
I'm going to say it with the questions.
No, no, you're going to go without me.

So we're going to have a brief conversation, as we do, a breakdown on one-on-one conversation like this at times, to practice active listening, where one person is going to speak for a few minutes and the other person just listens.
I'll ring the bell and the other person can speak and pay full attention.
And at the end, let it go.
Engage into yourself as much as you can, but then don't bring it up again with that person or someone else, whatever it is they say.
Topic.
You want what?
Reigetsu Susan Moon asks:
*What if a person who is lonely, single and lives alone without a family joins a Zen center for the company in order to feel a sense of belonging?
What if she likes Sangha Potlucks more than Zazen?*
The question for you is, what is sangha friendship and what would you like it to be?
The person who said the number first, go first.
